newsitem.title: SPAIN: FEATURE - Spain builders look abroad as public purse shuts.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Spain builders look abroad as public purse shuts.

text.p: Spain's building sector, still facing falling domestic production, is looking to consolidate activity abroad.

In the past, foreign markets represented a way to compensate cyclical falls in domestic demand. Now for the first time, companies are trying to consolidate their presence abroad, especially in Latin America, regardless of the domestic situation.
At the same time, they continue to diversify at home.

"Firms in the sector are looking for new opportunities inside the country, ranging from water to cleaning, and for new contracts in foreign countries," said Benito Vera, analyst at Salomon Brothers in London.

The sector has suffered since the boom years of the 1980s came to an end and public investment fell under the constraints of a tighter public purse. Public investment fell 14 percent in 1997 compared with the previous year.
In 1996, building production in Spain fell 0.7 percent in real terms and is expected to fall another 0.2 percent this year, according to a forecast by the sector association SEOPAN.
The sector has been trying to compensate by seeking overseas work. The number of foreign contracts won by Spanish firms rose 38 percent in 1996 and is expected to climb further in 1997, SEOPAN says.
"The construction sector in Spain is starting to mature. In a few years it will have to find new markets in which to expand," said a source at Fomento y Construcciones y Contratas.
One year ago, FCC reached a deal with its main competitor Dragados to develop business overseas. FCC took a six percent stake of Dragados while the latter took three percent of FCC.
In 1996, FCC had turnover of 429 billion pesetas ($2.9 billion), with a modest share of 26 billion pesetas made outside Spain.
Back in 1992, that figure was at 3.3 billion pesetas.
"We forecast that by the year 2,000, more than 10 percent (of our turnover) will come from beyond Spanish borders," the source at FCC said.
SMALLER FIRMS ALSO EYE FOREIGN CONTRACTS
Smaller companies have discovered a similar vocation.
"Orders in foreign countries are now key. They are leading sector (growth) as a strategic option," said Alicia Revenga, director of Seopan's international department.
"Medium-term we expect modest but constant growth for the sector. From 1999 the situation will improve but in 1997 and 1998 we'll likely see some uncertainty again," she added.
"So the recent trend is to increase their participation in international markets," she said.

Spanish firms are doing especially well in Latin America. Of their total business outside Spain, 47 percent comes from South and Central America, followed by Europe with 34 percent, and Africa with 11 percent.
"With domestic investment doing badly, Spanish firms are aiming to be in every relevant international project," said Ramon Carrascos, analyst at Ibersecurities brokerage in Madrid.

Almost all the big names of the Spanish construction sector have bid in a public auction in Colombia to build a network of new streets. Dragados won a $274 million contract at the beginning of July to build a Venezuelan hydro-electric plant.

Ferrovial, a smaller firm traditionally active in foreign business, said it already has investments in Chile, Colombia, and the Dominican Republic. It is taking part in the Colombian auction, for which the deadline is September 1.
At home, diversification ranges from waste disposal to water treatment, while firms are also restructuring to increase their financial muscle.
Spain's Development Ministry is currently studying new rules for awarding public works. These are expected to introduce stricter financial criteria as a pre-requisite to bidding for them.
"After the problems with Huarte they now want to be sure that building firms taking part in public contracts will not face financial problems," said an industry source.
Huarte is expected to make a profit this year after suspending payments in 1996. It is also planning to merge with Obrascon next year. ($ = 148.9 Spanish Pesetas)
